title: Alexander Graham Bell to Mabel Hubbard Bell, 27 Aug 1900, 'Unicode' commercial code telegram quoted in a letter (LoC magbell.04100117; catalogue 763)

documents.shelfmark: Library of Congress, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, magbell.04100117, image 1

plaintext.source: No decipherment in the letter or the LoC record; the letter says only that Mabel may 'have some fun in deciphering'. The key is the printed Unicode phrase book.

transcription.source: LoC master JPEG tile.loc.gov .../magbell/041/04100117/0001.jpg (1368x2148), read at display size
transcription.notes: Six code words and the clear name Bert. Sigma is struck out and Signinus written under it, so the By the People transcription's 'Signinas' signature is a misreading and Signinus is mid-message.

system.summary: Commercial phrase code: each Latin cypher word of 'Unicode' The Universal Telegraphic Phrase-Book stands for a printed phrase.
system.notes: The code book lists phrases alphabetically with Latin words in alphabetical order beside them; one word, one phrase.

prior_solution.where: No decipherment found in the LoC record, the By the People transcription or the project notes (checked 28 Oct 2026 and 29 Oct 2026).

solution.what: Read the task page (docs/solve/763.html). curl and WebFetch could not reach archive.org or loc.gov at first (network blocked); worked after the user changed the firewall.

Found the Unicode phrase book on archive.org (1896 ed. UnicodeUniversalTelegraphicPhraseBook; 1889 ed. unicodeuniversa00unkngoog) and looked the words up in the djvu text, pairing each word to its phrase by counting phrases and words per page.
Viewed LoC images 1-3. Message as sent: Roboro, Diallage, Siquando, Adalligo, Signinus (written under a struck-out Sigma), Promulgo, Bert.

Viewed the 1896 page images pp. 5, 35, 78, 88, 95 and 96: each word sits beside the phrase the OCR pairing gave. Promulgo is the betting phrase 'Put me £1,000 to win on —'; the letter does not explain it.
Plaintext: Telegram received. Glad to hear from you. Wrote to you by this morning's post. Am quite well, and writing by post. Weather very fine, sea quite smooth. [Put me £1,000 to win on —] Bert.

outcome.method_basis: The key is the printed Unicode phrase book (1896 edition), a public code book applied to the six code words; no key was recovered from the ciphertext.
outcome.fraction_read_source: reading.md: 6 of 6 code words valued; Bert is clear text and not counted

texts.summary: Bell, on the steamer Ulunda on the Thames, telegraphs his wife in a commercial code that she is to puzzle out; it says telegram received, glad to hear, wrote this morning, quite well, weather fine and sea smooth, plus one betting phrase that the letter does not explain.
texts.note: Promulgo is printed as a betting phrase and kept as printed; the letter does not explain it. It is a valued code word, not a hole.

reading_review.note: Read as a seven-word telegram of coherent sentences; Promulgo is a printed betting phrase the letter does not explain. Code values not re-checked against the 1896 edition here (archive.org unreachable on 31 Oct 2026).

outcome.notes: Code book entry for Promulgo is unexplained in context. The 1898 edition was not checked.

credits.note: the printed 'Unicode' Universal Telegraphic Phrase-Book (1896 edition; 1889 edition checked in its text layer only), a commercial code book of the time
